exercise1.prompt: Create an integer, a float and a string, then print all three

cases.name: creates a whole number
cases.call: len([v for v in list(globals().values()) if type(v) is int]) >= 1

cases.name: creates a decimal number
cases.call: len([v for v in list(globals().values()) if type(v) is float]) >= 1

cases.name: creates a string
cases.call: len([v for v in list(globals().values()) if type(v) is str]) >= 1

exercise1.hint: An integer has no decimal point (5), a float does (5.0), and a string is text in quotes ("five"). Assign each to its own variable name.

exercise2.hint: Multiply the two variables and print the result: print(price * quantity). Python prints 62.0 rather than 62 because price is a decimal.

questions.prompt: You write distance = 5.0. Which statement correctly describes the value stored in distance?
choices: It is an int because its mathematical value is a whole number
It is a string because distance is a name
It is a float, even though it has no fractional part
Its type cannot be known until it is printed
questions.explain: The literal 5.0 creates a float; 5 creates an int. A value can represent a whole number and still have floating-point type. type(distance) would confirm the type.

choices: Binds the name x to the value 5
Declares x as an integer variable permanently
questions.explain: A single = assigns. Testing for equality is ==, which is a different operator entirely.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a valid variable name?
questions.explain: Names cannot start with a digit, cannot contain hyphens, and cannot be Python keywords like class.

choices: It depends on how it is used
questions.explain: The quotes make it text. "5" + "5" gives "55", not 10.

questions.prompt: Match each idea to its meaning.
questions.hint: Look at the actual value: a decimal point and quotation marks change its type.
questions.explain: 12: An integer value. 12.5: A floating-point value. "12": A string value.

questions.label: Predict the first line of output (without surrounding quotes).
questions.prompt:
points = 10
bonus = points + 2
points = 20
print(points)
print(bonus)

First output line: ___
questions.hint: Trace each line in order and write down the current values. Stop at the first print call.
questions.explain: After line 1, points is 10. Line 2 calculates 12 and stores it as bonus. Line 3 reassigns points to 20 but does not recalculate bonus. Keep a small table of names and current values when tracing assignments.
